title: A New Story Starts
on_slide_text: Sage Valmiki has finished thinking about Rama's whole life in deep meditation. Now he is ready to tell the great story from the very start. He begins with the old Ikshvaku family that starts from Prajapati. King Ikshvaku laid its strong base long ago.
rationale: Opens the hook and sets Valmiki as teller starting the Ikshvaku tale from the beginning.

title: King Dasharatha of Ayodhya
on_slide_text: King Dasharatha rules the great city of Ayodhya. He comes from the Ikshvaku line and knows the holy Vedas. He has everything a king needs and thinks far ahead. He is strong and brave in war. All town and village people love him dearly.
rationale: Introduces Dasharatha as warrior, Veda-knower, and beloved lord of Ayodhya.

slide_label: Slide03 - A King Like a Sage
title: A King Like a Sage
on_slide_text: King Dasharatha performs holy sacrifices with care. He does his daily duties and controls his mind like a calm sage. People in all three worlds praise him. They call him a royal sage. He is a king outside and a sage inside.
rationale: Establishes his sacrifice, duty, and self-control as a royal sage.

title: Strong and True Protector
on_slide_text: King Dasharatha is full of strength and beats his foes. He keeps many good friends and controls his senses. He guards his people as kindly as Manu did long ago. He keeps his promise firmly. He rules Ayodhya with duty, wealth, and joy held together.
rationale: Shows his strength, friendship, sense-control, and rule by dharma, artha, and kama.

title: Happy People of Ayodhya
on_slide_text: The people of Ayodhya are happy and good at heart. They learn much and feel content with what they own. They hate greed and always speak the truth. No home lacks good food and goods. Every family owns horses, cows, grain, and wealth in plenty.
rationale: Shows contentment, truthfulness, and plenty as the base of city life.

title: Clean Hearts Everywhere
on_slide_text: You will not find a rude, cheating, lazy, or faithless person in Ayodhya. All men and women have fine manners and calm minds. They keep their senses quiet and stay cheerful. In work and conduct they shine like sages. They live a pure life with kind rules.
rationale: Continues the moral portrait of restrained, cheerful, sage-like citizens.

title: Dressed in Joy
on_slide_text: The people wear bright earrings, crowns, and flower garlands. They bathe daily and rub cool sandal paste on their arms. They smell sweet with perfumes and eat clean food. They love to give gifts to others. With bracelets on wrists, they keep their wishes calm.
rationale: Shows adornment, cleanliness, pure food, and charity held with self-control.

title: No Dark Homes
on_slide_text: Every home in Ayodhya keeps the holy fire burning. Every person joins true worship with right care. No one thinks small or mean thoughts. There is no thief in the streets. No one earns by wrong work or shameful ways.
rationale: Marks universal worship and absence of theft and wrong livelihood.

title: Wise and Giving Guides
on_slide_text: The calm priests of Ayodhya do their own duties well. They give gifts, read holy books, and take gifts only with care. None are liars, haters, or fools. All know the Vedas and keep strong vows. They give by the thousands and never act in fear.
rationale: Praises self-controlled Brahmanas learned in Vedas and generous in gifts.

title: Faces Full of Light
on_slide_text: Every man and woman in Ayodhya glows with health and beauty. No one looks dull or dim. All keep deep love for their king in their hearts. Each face smiles with cheer and kindness. Each person greets others with grace and honors the king truly.
rationale: Shows splendour, beauty, and heartfelt loyalty to the king.

title: Serving Gods and Guests
on_slide_text: People of all four groups honor wise guides first. They serve gods and welcome guests with love. They feel thankful, give freely, and stand brave and strong. They guard right living with courage. So worship and bravery live side by side in the city.
rationale: Unites gratitude, charity, and valour in service of gods and guests.

title: Long Happy Homes
on_slide_text: People in Ayodhya live long and follow truth each day. They stay together in full homes with joy. Sons, grandsons, and wives share one roof. Family lines grow strong in every house. Deep love binds them, so peace fills each kitchen and yard.
rationale: Depicts long life, joint families, and affection rooted in dharma.

title: Each Duty in Place
on_slide_text: Guides lead with wisdom and warriors guard with strength. Traders follow the warriors and workers serve all three with skill. Each group stands firm in its own work. King Dasharatha rules with great order. He guards the vast city as wisely as Manu did before.
rationale: Orders the four duties in harmony under Dasharatha's skilled rule.

title: Lions and Swift Horses
on_slide_text: Ayodhya is full of bright warriors like lions in a cave. They walk the straight path and fear no foe. They master bows and arms with skill. Fine horses from Kamboja, Bahlika, Vanayu, and Sindhu neigh in stalls. They run swift like the wind.
rationale: Displays lion-like warriors and famed horses as city strength.

title: Hills That Walk
on_slide_text: Huge elephants from Vindhya and snowy hills trumpet in Ayodhya. They are strong as moving mountains in rut. Bhadra, Mandra, and Mriga breeds stand with firm limbs. Some mix all three in noble lines. Like Airavata, they look like dark hills that walk.
rationale: Details mountain-like elephants of noble breeds guarding the city.

slide_label: Slide16 - The City None Can Win
title: The City None Can Win
on_slide_text: Ayodhya spreads two yojanas wide and none can conquer it. King Dasharatha crushes foes and shines like the moon among stars. Strong gates and bolts guard its walls. Fine palaces rise in rows. Thousands of happy people crowd its safe streets.
rationale: Closes the city portrait with its unconquerable name and moon-like king.

title: City Before Hero
question: Why does Valmiki describe the city of Ayodhya in such detail before introducing Rama himself — why the city before the hero?
answer: Because Rama is not dropped from the sky. He grows from a healthy home like a tree from good soil. When the king keeps his word, people speak truth. When the king controls himself, the city stays clean. So first check your home team. Live one good rule yourself before you ask others.
on_slide_text: Why show the city before the hero? Because a hero grows like a tree from good soil, not dropped from the sky. When the king keeps his word, people speak truth. When the king is calm, the city stays clean. Fix one rule in your home, and follow it first yourself.
rationale: Reflects that dharma is first a healthy system, then a person.

title: Joy With Control
question: Why is Dasharatha called in the same breath splendid like Indra-Kubera and self-controlled like a Maharshi — can enjoyment and restraint coexist?
answer: Yes, they can live together. Having nice things is not bad if you are not their slave. Dasharatha enjoys wealth but keeps it inside duty. His garlands and perfumes show care, not greed. Power helps people only when tied by self-control. Try it: enjoy one treat for seven days only inside a limit you set.
on_slide_text: How can a king enjoy riches and still be calm like a sage? Because holding things is different from being their slave. Dasharatha keeps wealth and joy inside duty. His perfumes and garlands show care, not greed. Pick one pleasure and enjoy it for seven days only inside your own limit.
rationale: Explains how wealth and desire bound by dharma become discipline, not lust.

title: No Greed No Theft
question: What does a city with no greedy, no thief, no liar mean — poetic exaggeration or psychological map?
answer: It is a map of the mind. Ayodhya means a place no enemy can win. The mind wins when it feels enough. Greed opens the door for lies and theft. When people feel content with their share, bad acts have no room to grow. Shut one greedy scroll for half an hour daily, and feel your mind grow strong.
on_slide_text: Is a city with no greed just a sweet dream? No, it is a map of your mind. Ayodhya means no enemy can win it. Greed opens the door for lies and theft. When hearts feel enough with their share, bad acts find no room. Close one greedy scroll for half an hour each day.
rationale: Reads Ayodhya as inner contentment that cuts crime at its root.

title: Teamwork Not Rank
question: How should we read Kshatriyas under Brahmanas and Vaishyas behind Kshatriyas today — is it mere praise of old hierarchy?
answer: Read it as clear teamwork, not high and low. Each group serves the other with a gift. Guides give wisdom, guards give safety, traders give food, helpers join all with care. Today all say equal but fight for the same job. Write your three life roles and do one fixed duty for each this week without complaint.
on_slide_text: Why do groups follow each other — is it unfair rank? No, it is clear teamwork for all. Guides give wisdom, guards give safety, traders give food, helpers join with care. All serve gods and guests together. Write your three life jobs and do one true duty for each this week.
rationale: Reframes varna as mutual service and role-clarity for today.

title: Beauty Is Discipline
question: Why so much adornment in the city of dharma — sandal-perfume, earrings-garlands and rutting elephants-horses; does the path to liberation not go through simplicity?
answer: Because true control is not sad, it is beautiful. Bathing, sweet smell, clean food, and giving sit in one line. Care for the body becomes prayer when done with grace, not greed. Kindness needs strong guards to last. Pick one lovely habit — sit calm two minutes after bath or eat with thanks — and make duty shine.
on_slide_text: Why wear perfume and jewels on the path of duty? Because true control is not sad, it is beautiful. Clean baths, sweet smells, and giving grow together. Strength guards kindness so peace can last. Keep one lovely habit — sit calm two minutes after bathing or eat food with thanks.
rationale: Lands the sharpest insight that restraint shines as beauty guarded by strength.
